questions.question_text: Use the unit circle to find $\cos180^\circ$.

options.why: Used the $y$-coordinate, which gives $\sin180^\circ$, instead of the $x$-coordinate.
Used the point at $0^\circ$ instead of the point at $180^\circ$.
Confused cosine with tangent at a vertical radius; cosine is defined at every angle.

questions.solution_text:
At $180^\circ$, the unit-circle point is $(-1,0)$.
Cosine is the $x$-coordinate, so $\cos180^\circ=-1$.

questions.question_text: For an angle of inclination $\theta=205^{\circ}$, which of the trigonometric ratios are negative?

options.why: Assumed tangent is negative in the third quadrant, but $\tan\theta=\frac{y}{x}>0$ in Q3.
Assumed cosine is positive in the third quadrant; in Q3 both $x<0$ and $y<0$, so $\cos<0$.
Overlooked that the ratio of two negative coordinates $\frac{y}{x}$ gives a positive tangent.

questions.solution_text:
$205^{\circ}$ lies in the third quadrant where $x<0$ and $y<0$.
Therefore $\sin 205^{\circ}<0$, $\cos 205^{\circ}<0$, and $\tan 205^{\circ}>0$.

questions.question_text: Use the unit circle to find $\sin270^\circ$.

options.why: Used the point at $90^\circ$ instead of the point at $270^\circ$.
Used the $x$-coordinate, which gives $\cos270^\circ$, instead of the $y$-coordinate.
Confused sine with tangent; tangent is undefined at $270^\circ$, but sine is the defined $y$-coordinate.

questions.solution_text:
At $270^\circ$, the unit-circle point is $(0,-1)$.
Sine is the $y$-coordinate, so $\sin270^\circ=-1$.

questions.question_text: A point $P$ lies on a circle of radius $6$ centred at the origin, with angle of inclination $270^\circ$. What are the coordinates of $P$?

options.why: Used the unit-circle coordinates without multiplying by the radius $6$.
Swapped the coordinates; cosine gives $x=0$ and sine gives $y=-6$.
Used the positive $y$-axis at $90^\circ$ instead of the negative $y$-axis at $270^\circ$.

questions.solution_text:
$x=6\cos270^\circ=0$
$y=6\sin270^\circ=-6$
$P(0,-6)$, on the negative $y$-axis at distance $6$ from the origin.

questions.question_text: Use the unit circle to find $\tan90^\circ$.

options.why: Reversed the ratio to $x/y=0/1$; tangent is $y/x$.
Used the $y$-coordinate, which gives sine, instead of the ratio $y/x$.
Used the sine value at $270^\circ$ instead of evaluating tangent at $90^\circ$.

questions.solution_text:
At $90^\circ$, the unit-circle point is $(0,1)$.
$\tan\theta=y/x$ requires division by zero here, so $\tan90^\circ$ is undefined.

options.why: Selected the quadrants where sine is positive ($y>0$) rather than tangent ($y/x>0$).
Selected the quadrants where cosine is positive ($x>0$) rather than tangent ($y/x>0$).
Selected the quadrants where tangent is negative ($x$ and $y$ have opposite signs).

questions.solution_text: $\tan\theta=\dfrac{y}{x}$ is positive where $x$ and $y$ have the same sign: Q1 ($x>0,y>0$) and Q3 ($x<0,y<0$).

questions.question_text:
An angle $\theta$ is located in the fourth quadrant.
What are the signs of $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$, and $\tan\theta$?

options.why: Gave the signs for the first quadrant; in the fourth quadrant $y<0$.
Gave the signs for the second quadrant where $x<0$ and $y>0$.
Gave the signs for the third quadrant where both $x<0$ and $y<0$.

questions.question_text: A point $P$ lies on a circle of radius $4\sqrt{5}$ centred at the origin, with angle of inclination $180^\circ$. What are the exact coordinates of $P$?

options.why: Dropped the negative sign from $\cos180^\circ=-1$, placing the point on the positive $x$-axis.
Swapped sine and cosine when forming the coordinates.
Used the unit-circle coordinates without scaling by the radius $4\sqrt{5}$.

questions.solution_text:
$x=4\sqrt{5}\cos180^\circ=-4\sqrt{5}$
$y=4\sqrt{5}\sin180^\circ=0$
$P(-4\sqrt{5},0)$.
The point lies on the negative $x$-axis and its distance from the origin is $\sqrt{80}=4\sqrt{5}$.

questions.question_text: A point $P$ lies on a circle of radius $2\sqrt{6}$ centred at the origin, with angle of inclination $270^\circ$. What are the exact coordinates of $P$?

options.why: Used sine for the $x$-coordinate and cosine for the $y$-coordinate.
Dropped the negative sign from $\sin270^\circ=-1$.
Used the unit-circle coordinates without multiplying by the radius $2\sqrt{6}$.

questions.solution_text:
$x=2\sqrt{6}\cos270^\circ=0$
$y=2\sqrt{6}\sin270^\circ=-2\sqrt{6}$
$P(0,-2\sqrt{6})$.
The point lies on the negative $y$-axis and its distance from the origin is $\sqrt{24}=2\sqrt{6}$.
